To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) circulating thymic hormone activity (CTHA) is present in the serum of normal children; (2) CTHA is absent in the serum of children with severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) and in the serum of two infants with DiGeorge's syndrome; (3) CTHA rises in the serum after successful reconstitution in SCID; (4) CTHA may be absent in the serum in SCID patients with adenosine deaminase deficiency

the circulating thymic hormone activity in children with severe combined immunodeficiency is very low, whereas in those with adenosine-deam-inase deficiency it is high, and that the activity rises after successful bone marrow transplantation.

the thymic hormone is detectable in the plasma of normal children, but not in the plasma of infants with severe combined immunodeficiency, and that the plasma of infants reconstituted with a thymus or a bone-marrow graft becomes positive for thymic hormone.
